Force Job Leak Detection (with stack traces) on editor startup

Unity resets Jobs ▶ Leak Detection to a lower level every time the editor restarts. While this is on, Basis re-applies “Enabled With Stack Trace” on each editor load so native/job leaks keep reporting full stack traces. Turn it off to disable leak detection (no overhead).
Allow HTTP on the local network

Basis picks the scheme per host: IP literals, localhost, single-label host names and .local/.lan/.internal/.home.arpa use http://, everything else uses https://. This grants the platform permission that choice needs — insecureHttpOption on Windows and Linux, usesCleartextTraffic on Android/Quest, and NSAllowsLocalNetworking on iOS and macOS (private and .local hosts only; public hosts stay TLS-only).

Assembly Definitions (asmdef) — How to hook into Basis

Create Assets/YourGame/Editor/YourGame.Editor.asmdef, tick Include Platforms → Editor, and reference YourGame.Runtime (+ any Basis Editor assemblies you need).
Tip: To find the exact Basis assembly to reference, click any Basis script and check its Assembly Definition in the Inspector. Add only what you need.

Unsubscribing may not remove the handler

Each time an interpreted method is used as a delegate it becomes a fresh host wrapper, so the one you remove may not be the one you added. For a publisher that outlives your script, poll instead of subscribing.
Once a type is whitelisted, every public method on it is callable unless that type also appears in a method restriction. Adding a type grants more than it looks like.
Parameter and return types are checked too
A method can pass the name check and still be refused because one of its parameters, generic arguments or its return type is not whitelisted. This is the most confusing way for a call to fail.
They have different declaring types, and only the GameObject one is restricted. The avatar and scene sandboxes allow the hierarchy walk; the prop sandbox does not. The this. spelling always works.
Unconverted scripts are destroyed on load
Any component that is neither cilboxed nor approved in ContentPolice is removed when the content loads. Converting a script and approving a component are two separate steps.
The compiler folds a const into the instruction stream, so no field access is ever emitted for it. Only real fields need listing, and field access is default-deny.
Avatar scripts run on other people's clients
Every cilboxed script on a remote avatar ticks locally, up to the per-avatar behaviour limit. Anything the avatar sandbox allows, a stranger's avatar can do on your machine.

A raw pointer or runtime handle would let a script hand an arbitrary address to any native-interop method whose other parameters are allowed. Refused before the allow list is consulted, so no wildcard can bring them back.

The indexer is bounds-checked only in the editor and development builds, so in a shipped player an out-of-range write would be an arbitrary native write. Reading is still available through ToArray and CopyTo.
Properties are methods: add get_X or set_X under method restrictions instead. Constants need no entry and are not listed.
